(Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. attachment.content:
- angle-generator: Turn a company update into 3-7 structurally distinct, journalist-shaped story angles. Runs the fact through proven newsroom lenses (perspective, abstraction, news values, data, contrarian, news peg) and refuses rephrasings, invented facts, named-journalist guesses, and AI-marketing slop. - User has company news but no story yet: funding, launch, hire, partnership, customer milestone, data point, weak pitch angle, or a newsjack-detector handoff that needs story angles before pitch drafting or media-list building.
- codebase-design: Shared vocabulary for designing deep modules. Use when the user wants to design or improve a module's interface, find deepening opportunities, decide where a seam goes, make code more testable or AI-navigable, or when another skill needs the deep-module vocabulary.
- coverage-tracker: Run a Google Alerts-style keyword coverage tracker. Uses news-search for recent keyword queries, lets the LLM dedupe and classify real features versus junk, stores decisions in SQLite, and alerts only on new real coverage. - User wants to run coverage alerts, check new mentions, track press coverage, monitor brand/company keyword coverage, or execute a previously configured coverage tracker.
- coverage-tracker-setup: Set up a lightweight Google Alerts-style coverage tracker for any number of keywords. Creates a tracker config with each keyword and what it actually means, then hands recurrence to the user's agent harness. - User wants to create, configure, or update coverage alerts, brand/company mention tracking, Google Alert-style monitoring, or keyword coverage tracking. Use this instead of newsjack-monitor-setup when the job is to track coverage of the user's own keywords rather than find newsjacking opportunities.
- crisis-holding: Draft crisis holding statements, journalist Q&A posture, and what-not-to-say guidance from confirmed incident facts, with a hard legal-counsel gate. Builds each statement through proven crisis-comms frameworks (holding-statement anatomy, SCCT, CAP order, the legitimate non-answer, bridge/flag/block). - User describes a brewing or live incident involving product safety, data security, personnel, regulatory exposure, outages, viral backlash, executive statements, third parties, or a newsjacking landmine. Not for launches, marketing copy, or ordinary press releases.
- design-an-interface: Generate multiple radically different interface designs for a module using parallel sub-agents. Use when user wants to design an API, explore interface options, compare module shapes, or mentions "design it twice".
- diagnosing-bugs: Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow.
- domain-modeling: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when the user wants to pin down domain terminology or a ubiquitous language, record an architectural decision, or when another skill needs to maintain the domain model.
- fact-check: Extract factual claims from PR copy, verify each claim independently, attach concrete citations, and warn when certainty is low. Runs each claim through proven newsroom verification methods (lateral reading, source-tier climbing, provenance pillars, triangulation, calibrated rating) and puts the burden of proof on the speaker. Use before a pitch, press release, reactive comment, DM, or other journalist-facing draft is trusted or sent. - User asks to verify facts, check sources, cite claims, assess whether a draft is safe to send, or another newsjack skill needs a pre-send factual accuracy gate.
- find-journalists: Create, inspect, edit, enrich, and share fit-checked media lists for newsjack campaigns. Uses the optional Medialyst MCP server when available, and falls back to a local artifact when the cloud substrate is not configured. - User asks to build, generate, refine, dedupe, inspect, enrich, manage, or share a media list; asks for journalists for a pitch or newsjack angle; asks to add columns, notes, views, or share links to a media list; or another newsjack skill has produced journalist shapes that need real recipient discovery.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- grilling: Interview the user relentlessly about a plan or design. Use when the user wants to stress-test a plan before building, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.
- headroom: Use when the context window is getting full (>60%), when handling large logs, or when processing massive code files.
- humanizer: Remove signs of AI-generated writing from text. Use when editing or reviewing
text to make it sound more natural and human-written. Based on Wikipedia's
comprehensive "Signs of AI writing" guide. Detects and fixes patterns including:
inflated symbolism, promotional language, superficial -ing analyses, vague
attributions, em dash overuse, rule of three, AI vocabulary words, negative
parallelisms, and excessive conjunctive phrases.
- journalist-fit-check: Gate a pitch against one journalist at a time. Runs the pair through proven media-relations checks (last-10-bylines audit, 90-day topic sweep, beat-vs-angle-vs-one-off, the 5 forms of journalism, source-mirror, stated-preferences, database triangulation) and returns fit, soft-fit, no-fit, or unknown with a real recent anchor and specific edits. - User asks whether a specific journalist is a fit for a pitch, wants a pre-send relevance check, tries to add one journalist to a media list, or asks 'should I pitch this person?'
- meanest-editor: Roast a pitch or press release with the eye of a veteran PR director. Honest, sharp, constructive — never cruel for its own sake. - User asks for a pitch critique, press release review, 'roast my draft', 'is this any good', or shares PR copy and wants honest feedback.
- news-search: Search current news for a topic, company, competitor, or hook and return dated, attributed articles. Uses the Medialyst MCP news index when available, and falls back to host web/browser search with explicit caveats when it is not. - User asks to search the news, find recent coverage, check who has written about a topic, or pull article evidence; or another Newsjack skill needs dated, attributed news results (coverage-tracker, story-origin-check, newsworthiness-check, find-journalists, newsjack-detector). Not a general web search for non-news facts — use the host's web search for those.
- newsjack-detector: Monitor current news and reaction signals, then decide which are credible newsjacking opportunities for a client. Uses the local monitoring engine for evidence, but the skill owns PR judgment, brand safety, standing, decay, angle fit, and handoff. - User wants to monitor news for pitchable hooks, find newsjacking opportunities, react to breaking industry news, watch competitors/topics, or decide whether a current signal is worth turning into an angle or reactive comment.
- newsjack-monitor-setup: Set up a newsjack monitoring profile for a company so newsjack-detector can run on a schedule. Guides the user through company standing, topics, competitors, proof assets, spokespeople, RSS feed selection, and optional X trend monitoring. - User wants to set up monitoring, create or configure a monitor profile, schedule recurring newsjack scans, choose RSS/news feeds, or prepare a profile for newsjack-detector. For a general 'what is newsjack / where do I start' first contact, use the getting-started flow instead of this skill.
- newsjack-triage: Consolidate freshness-gated newsjack signals and route them by client standing before angle generation. Collapses any remaining same-story duplicates, decides strong/partial/none standing with a journalist-shape sanity check, and sorts each story into pitch_ready, big_story (always-surfaced suggestion), or watch. Never writes angles or pitches, and never drops a fresh big story. - Run as the standing-triage stage of the newsjack-detector pipeline, after the deterministic freshness gate (origin-apply) and before angle-generator. Use whenever a pool of fresh candidate signals needs standing judgment and final same-story consolidation before expensive angle work.
- newsworthiness-check: Score whether a news event is worth newsjacking, or whether a user's pitch idea is actually newsworthy to journalists. Uses calibrated anchors, hard anti-inflation rules, standing checks, timing windows, and brand-safety kill switches. - User asks if something is newsworthy, worth pitching, worth newsjacking, likely to get press, strong enough for journalists, or asks for a score/rubric/check on a current event, company announcement, pitch idea, or news hook.
- openfort: Always use this skill when the user wants to explore Openfort documentation, browse SDK source code, or use Openfort MCP tools. This is the general-purpose Openfort platform skill — use it for documentation lookup, source code navigation, and CLI operations. For building with embedded wallets, use the openfort-embedded-wallet skill. For backend wallets, use the openfort-backend-wallets skill. Trigger on: "Openfort docs", "search Openfort", "Openfort source code", "openfort CLI", "MCP tools", "Openfort SDK source", or general Openfort platform questions.
- openfort-embedded-wallet: Always use this skill when the user asks about embedded wallets, client-side wallets, user-facing wallets, wallet integration in React/React Native/Swift/Unity/JS apps, or non-custodial wallets with Openfort. Covers all client SDKs. Trigger on: "embedded wallet", "client wallet", "user wallet", "@openfort/react", "@openfort/react-native", "OpenfortSwift", "openfort-csharp-unity", "@openfort/openfort-js", "OpenfortProvider", "OpenfortButton", "wallet setup", "wallet integration", "passkey recovery", "gasless transaction client", "auth modal", or any client-side wallet operation with Openfort.
- pr-strategist: Opinionated startup-PR strategist that helps founders figure out audience, positioning, news pegs, and drumbeat before any tactical PR. Refuses outlet-naming-before-audience, mass blasts, vanity metrics, and premature agency spend. - User asks how to get press, get coverage, build a PR strategy, pitch a publication, or do PR for their startup — without first having a goal, audience, positioning, and a news peg.
- qa: Interactive QA session where user reports bugs or issues conversationally, and the agent files GitHub issues. Explores the codebase in the background for context and domain language. Use when user wants to report bugs, do QA, file issues conversationally, or mentions "QA session".
- reactive-comment: Triage inbound journalist source queries and draft a response only when the user's expertise is a real fit. Runs each query through proven source-request lenses (4-gate fit triage, credential-standing test, deadline read, BLUF/inverted-pyramid drafting), kills weak fits, asks for missing proof, and never auto-sends. - User shares a HARO, Source of Sources, Qwoted, Featured, Help A B2B Writer, JournoRequest, or similar source request and wants to know whether to respond or wants a response drafted.
- relevance-coarse-filter: Cheap, high-recall first-pass filter that removes obvious junk from a detector candidate pool before expensive story-origin research and PR judgment. Decides keep, monitor_only, or reject — never ranks, writes angles, verifies dates, or decides whether to pitch. - Use as the coarse relevance pass of the newsjack-detector pipeline, or whenever a candidate signal pool needs cheap junk removal before expensive newsworthiness judgment. Designed to run on a low-cost model.
- search-product: Search AliExpress by product name / keyword and return a structured list of matching listings — productId, canonical detail URL, title, current price, list price, discount %, rating, sold count, and badges. Read-only.
- story-origin-check: Recover the first public timestamp and canonical major coverage for a newsjacking signal, then decide whether newer coverage is the same story, a different story, or a materially new development. - Use before deterministic freshness gating, before sending beta cron output, or whenever evidence comes from aggregators, syndication partners, copied wire articles, rewritten secondary coverage, or search results with suspiciously recent timestamps.
- tdd: Test-driven development. Use when the user wants to build features or fix bugs test-first, mentions "red-green-refactor", or wants integration tests.
- voice-extractor: Capture a user's real writing voice from 5-20 prior samples, store a local voice.yaml fingerprint, and enforce it on newsjack drafts so AI tells disappear. Measures voice with named stylometry lenses (Burrows's Delta function-word vector, MATTR lexical diversity, sentence-length burstiness, Biber Dimension-1 register, opener-POS profile, punctuation rates) and gates drafts against the fingerprint as bands, not vibes. - User asks to set up, refresh, check, or enforce a newsjack voice fingerprint; user says drafts sound generic or AI-written; another newsjack drafting skill needs sender-voice constraints before returning copy.
- solidity-auditor: Security audit of Solidity code while you develop. Trigger on "audit", "check this contract", "review for security". Modes - default (full repo), DEEP (+ adversarial reasoning), or a specific filename.
- entry-point-analyzer:entry-points: Identifies state-changing entry points in smart contracts
- claude-hud:setup: Configure claude-hud as your statusline
- claude-hud:configure: Configure HUD display options (layout, language, presets, display elements) while preserving advanced manual overrides
- frontend-design:frontend-design: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
- adversarial-spec:adversarial-spec: Iteratively refine a product spec by debating with multiple LLMs (GPT, Gemini, Grok, etc.) until all models agree. Use when user wants to write or refine a specification document using adversarial development.
- entry-point-analyzer:entry-point-analyzer: Analyzes smart contract codebases to identify state-changing entry points for security auditing. Detects externally callable functions that modify state, categorizes them by access level (public, admin, role-restricted, contract-only), and generates structured audit reports. Excludes view/pure/read-only functions. Use when auditing smart contracts (Solidity, Vyper, Solana/Rust, Move, TON, CosmWasm) or when asked to find entry points, audit flows, external functions, access control patterns, or privileged operations.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). state:	OPEN

## What to build

A Subscriber buys Fraction Tokens in a primary offering using a **mock regulated stablecoin (mock ERC-20)**, settled as atomic delivery-versus-payment: tokens and cash swap in one transaction or the whole thing reverts. Proceeds are released to the Vendor, the Subscriber's portfolio updates (read model in Neon), and settlement events are emitted for later fiat reconciliation. Primary-offering parameters (price/discount, caps, per-investor limits) are configurable per cell.

Real Ctrl Alt stablecoin + fiat on/off-ramp replaces the mock later — tracked separately (see the `ctrl-alt-integration` issue).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Mock stablecoin + DvP subscription contract; buy is atomic (token+cash or revert), tested
- [ ] Per-cell offering parameters (price/discount, caps, limits) enforced
- [ ] Vendor receives proceeds on settlement
- [ ] Subscription UI shows price/discount/fees/balance and confirms DvP
- [ ] Portfolio reflects holdings + cost basis; settlement events emitted

## Blocked by

- #2

Refs: BRD v2 Epic 4; ADR-0004, ADR-0005.

# 4. Atomic stablecoin DvP default, off-chain fiat fallback; multi-option key custody

Date: 2026-06-21
Status: Accepted — for R1 the stablecoin/fiat rails are mocked (ADR-0005) and wallet custody is self-custody only (ADR-0006). Multi-option custody deferred.

## Context

When a Subscriber buys, or a Shotgun/Drag/Tag forces a sale, tokens and cash must change hands. An
off-chain-fiat-with-event-hooks design is non-atomic and inherits the 48h/72h settlement-failure
risk the working paper explicitly worries about. The working paper (def. 31, §7.3) already leans
toward atomic stablecoin settlement.

Separately, retail Subscribers cannot be assumed to manage seed phrases, yet crypto-native
institutions want self-custody and some institutions want full third-party custody.

## Decision

**Settlement:** Atomic on-chain **DvP using a regulated stablecoin / tokenized deposit** (e.g.
RLUSD or a Ctrl Alt-issued token) is the default rail — token and cash swap or revert together in
one transaction; the contracts escrow stablecoin during Shotgun/Drag windows. **Off-chain fiat**
remains a fallback for large institutional tickets, reconciled via emitted events. Fiat on/off-ramp
and stablecoin mint/redeem are the Issuer's responsibility (labeled dependency).

**Key custody:** Support **all three** wallet types as a per-Subscriber choice, all whitelistable
through the same ONCHAINID registry:
1. Embedded account-abstraction smart wallet (passkey/social login + recovery) — recommended retail
   default;
2. Self-custody EOA (MetaMask/hardware) — crypto-native/institutional;
3. Issuer custodial wallet — institutions wanting full custody.

## Consequences

- Core contracts must implement DvP/escrow, not mere event emission — larger but safer contract
  surface.
- Lost-key recovery must rebind an ONCHAINID to a new address without burning underlying tokens.
- The platform integrates an embedded-wallet provider and must abstract over wallet type in the UI.

19	///         Registry at Ctrl Alt's claim-issuer address and stop deploying this contract.
20	///

22	///      ADR-0005, and CLAUDE.md "Mocks & how to replace them".

24	    /// @param initialManagementKey The address whose ECDSA signatures this issuer will treat

out = "out"
libs = ["lib"]

auto_detect_solc = true

via_ir = true

I'm noticing a discrepancy between the issue title and its description — the title references cell creation and token issuance, but the body actually describes a subscription and delivery-versus-payment flow, which seems to belong to a different epic. The references section appears to be cut off.

Looking at the acceptance criteria, it's clear this is really about implementing a DvP subscription system with a mock stablecoin. I need to build the smart contracts for a mock stablecoin and a primary offering contract that handles atomic token-for-cash swaps with per-cell offering parameters, vendor settlement, and proper event emission. On the frontend, I'll create a subscription interface showing pricing and fees with DvP confirmation, plus a portfolio view tracking holdings and cost basis.

Now I'm thinking through the DvP mechanics with ERC-3643 compliance — the offering contract needs to be whitelisted as an identity in the registry to hold and transfer tokens, and subscribers must also be whitelisted to receive them. I could either have the offering contract hold a pre-allocated supply of tokens and transfer them atomically with stablecoin pulls, or have it act as a token agent and mint directly to subscribers. The transfer approach seems cleaner since it mirrors the "tokens and cash swap" described in the requirements.

For the implementation, I'll design a PrimaryOffering contract that manages multiple offerings keyed by ID, with the offering contract itself registered as a verified identity in the IdentityRegistry so it can hold and transfer ERC-3643 tokens.

Defining the contract structure... The tokens transfer to the investor atomically, and ERC-3643 reverts if they're not whitelisted, preserving the transaction's all-or-nothing guarantee. I'll update the sold and purchased counters and emit the Subscribed event to mark settlement. Since the vendor receives payment directly during the subscription, that satisfies the settlement requirement—I could emit a separate ProceedsReleased event for clarity, though escrow and conditional flows are better suited to a later phase. For the offering to hold inventory, the contract needs to be whitelisted as an ERC-3643 token holder, which is complex; instead, I'm considering making the PrimaryOffering a token agent that can mint directly to subscribers, which is cleaner for this initial implementation.

Minting new tokens to subscribers actually mirrors a primary issuance more accurately than pre-funding inventory, and it keeps the DvP atomic—the stablecoin transfer and token mint happen together or both revert. I'll grant the offering the agent role through the token's addAgent function during deployment, then the subscription flow pulls stablecoins to the vendor and mints fractions to the subscriber in a single atomic transaction.

For the MockStablecoin, I'm creating a simple ERC-20 with a public mint function to simulate the on-ramp, using 6 decimals like USDC. The token itself has 0 decimals for fractions. I'll also add optional fee handling to the offering—a feeBps that gets applied on top of the discounted price and sent to a feeRecipient, keeping it straightforward without overcomplicating the scope.

Now I need to look at the existing web app structure—the contract utilities, wagmi setup, database patterns, and components—to understand how to build the frontend consistently with what's already there.

The subscribe function needs to validate the offering is active, check quantity and per-investor limits against the cap, compute costs, transfer stablecoin to the vendor and fees to the recipient, mint fraction tokens atomically to the subscriber, and emit events. I'll use ReentrancyGuard to protect against reentrancy attacks, and the contract needs to be registered as a token agent for each offering's token by the token owner.

Finally, I'll write a deployment script that sets up both the mock stablecoin and the PrimaryOffering contract, then wires the offering as a token agent. The frontend loads offering and token addresses from environment config, then the subscription panel displays pricing details, balance, and a live quote before executing the DvP transaction and posting settlement data to the portfolio API. The portfolio system uses a read model in Neon to track holdings and cost basis derived from settlement history, with both memory and database implementations behind a shared interface. For testing, I'm focusing on the natural TDD seams: the Solidity contract with comprehensive tests, and the pure cost-basis aggregation logic in TypeScript written test-first.

For the cost calculation, I'm defining the formula precisely—gross amount times price, then applying discount and fee percentages to determine what the subscriber pays versus what the vendor receives. Starting with the frontend portfolio read-model, I'll build out the cost-basis calculation as a pure function with tests first, then set up the settlements repository with both in-memory and Neon database options behind a shared interface, wire it into an API route, and finally create the UI layer. For the data model, I'm defining a settlement record that captures each confirmed subscription with fields for the chain, offering, fraction token address, investor wallet, vendor, and quantity.

For cost basis aggregation, I need to handle bigint-as-string amounts carefully since fractions have zero decimals and stablecoin amounts are in smallest units. I'll create a pure function that groups settlements by investor and token, summing quantities and total paid amounts using BigInt arithmetic, then computing the average unit cost as floor division. The holdings output will include quantity, total cost, and average unit cost all as bigint strings so the UI can format them with proper decimal places.

Now I'm setting up the repository pattern with a shared interface, memory implementation for testing, and Neon implementation for production, following the existing project structure.

10	/// @title PrimaryOffering
11	/// @notice Atomic delivery-versus-payment (DvP) primary subscription for RoughNet cells
12	///         (BRD Epic 4; ADR-0004). A Subscriber buys Fraction Tokens by paying a regulated
13	///         stablecoin: in a single transaction the stablecoin moves to the Vendor (and an
14	///         optional platform fee to the fee recipient) and the Fraction Tokens are delivered to
15	///         the Subscriber by minting the primary issuance. If any leg fails — most importantly if
16	///         the Subscriber is not whitelisted in the ERC-3643 Identity Registry, or has
17	///         insufficient stablecoin — the whole transaction reverts. Tokens and cash swap together
18	///         or not at all (FR4.1).
19	///
20	///         Primary-offering parameters are configured per cell by the platform operator
21	///         (Facilitator role in R1): unit price, discount, optional platform fee, total cap, and
22	///         a per-investor limit (FR4.4). Settlement events are emitted for the Issuer's banking
23	///         reconciliation and the off-chain portfolio read-model (FR4.3).
24	///
25	///         For R1 the stablecoin is a {MockStablecoin} and there is no Ctrl Alt rail; production
26	///         swaps in the Ctrl Alt-issued stablecoin behind the same {IERC20} interface (issue #12,
27	///         ADR-0005). Escrowed / conditional settlement and the fiat-wire fallback leg
28	///         (FR4.2/FR4.8) are governance-window concerns deferred to Epic 7; primary subscription
29	///         settles immediately and atomically to the Vendor.
30	///
31	/// @dev This contract must hold the ERC-3643 token agent role for each offering's token so it can
32	///      {IToken.mint}. The token owner grants it via `token.addAgent(address(this))` after the
33	///      offering is created (see DeployOffering.s.sol). Delivery is a primary mint rather than a
34	///      transfer of held inventory, which is the accurate model for a *primary* offering and
35	///      avoids the offering needing its own whitelisted ONCHAINID.

47	    struct Offering {
48	        IToken token; // ERC-3643 Fraction Token for the cell (delivery leg)
49	        address vendor; // receives the subscription proceeds (FR4.3)
50	        uint256 unitPrice; // stablecoin smallest-units per whole Fraction Token, pre-discount
51	        uint16 discountBps; // primary-offering discount applied to the price (FR4.4)
52	        uint16 feeBps; // optional platform fee charged on top of the net price
53	        address feeRecipient; // receives the platform fee (ignored when feeBps == 0)
54	        uint256 cap; // max total Fraction Tokens sellable in this offering (FR4.4)
55	        uint256 perInvestorLimit; // max Fraction Tokens a single wallet may buy (0 = no limit)
56	        uint256 sold; // running total of Fraction Tokens sold
57	        bool active; // subscriptions only succeed while active
58	    }
59

61	    Offering[] private _offerings;

63	    /// @notice Fraction Tokens bought per offering per investor (enforces perInvestorLimit).

1	<!-- cspell:words Copilot CodeRabbit coderabbitai Qodo Carini oneline cspell -->
2	
3	# PR Review Handling Guide
4	
5	Use this guide when working through automated PR feedback from Copilot, CodeRabbit, Vercel, Qodo, or similar reviewers.
6	
7	## Goals
8	
9	- Identify only the comments that belong to the latest review cycle.
10	- Verify each comment before changing code.
11	- Fix correctness, security, accessibility, and maintainability issues first.
12	- Avoid circular review loops by consolidating repeated patterns into one clean design.
13	- Stop when Copilot returns no new comments, or after 10 review-fix loops.
14	
15	## Review loop policy
16	
17	After requesting a Copilot review:
18	
19	1. Wait 4 minutes, then check whether a newer Copilot review exists.
20	2. If it is not ready, wait up to 10 more times for 2 minutes each.
21	3. Once comments arrive, read the review summary and all new inline comments.
22	4. Validate each comment:
23	   - If it is correct, fix it.
24	   - If it is a nit only, consider whether it is worth changing.
25	   - If it conflicts with an earlier comment, stop and choose the cleaner architecture instead of toggling code back and forth.
26	   - If several comments share the same root cause, make one consolidated design fix.
27	5. Run the project verification commands appropriate for the changed files.
28	6. Commit, push, and request a new Copilot review.
29	7. Repeat up to 10 times.
30	8. Exit early when Copilot returns `generated no new comments`.
31	
32	Do not continue an unbounded loop. If the 10-loop limit is reached and Copilot still reports issues, summarize the remaining pattern and recommend a deliberate consolidation pass.
33	
34	## Review data model
35	
36	- **Review event**: top-level review submission with timestamp and summary body.
37	- **Inline comment**: file-specific comment under `/pulls/<PR>/comments`.
38	- **Issue comment**: timeline comment under `/issues/<PR>/comments`.
39	- **Review body**: some bots, especially CodeRabbit, place nested actionable details in the review body instead of inline comments.
40	
41	Inline comments can be associated with a later review event even if timestamps are close together. Always compare both commit time and review submission time.
42	
43	## Quick setup
44	
45	```bash
46	PR=2
47	REPO=$(gh repo view --json owner,name -q '.owner.login + "/" + .name')
48	```
49	
50	For fork PRs, pass the repo explicitly when needed:
51	
52	```bash
53	REPO=SvenMeyer/front-pro
54	PR=2
55	```
56	
57	## Find the latest commit and reviews
58	
59	```bash
60	# Latest local commit with timestamp.
61	git log --oneline -1 --pretty=format:'%h %ai %s'
62	
63	# Latest PR commits from GitHub.
64	gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --json commits \
65	  --jq '.commits[-5:][] | {oid, committedDate, messageHeadline}'
66	
67	# Latest Copilot reviews.
68	gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --json reviews \
69	  --jq '[.reviews[] | select(.author.login == "copilot-pull-request-reviewer") | {submittedAt,state,body}] | sort_by(.submittedAt) | reverse | .[0:5]'
70	```
71	
72	A clean Copilot result looks like:
73	
74	```text
75	Copilot reviewed X out of Y changed files in this pull request and generated no new comments.
76	```
77	
78	## Fetch new Copilot comments
79	
80	Use the review timestamp or latest pushed commit timestamp as the lower bound.
81	
82	```bash
83	SINCE="2026-06-07T13:42:00Z"
84	
85	gh api "/repos/$REPO/pulls/$PR/comments?per_page=100" \
86	  --jq '[.[] | select(.created_at >= "'"$SINCE"'" and (.user.login == "Copilot" or .user.login == "copilot-pull-request-reviewer")) | {id, created_at, updated_at, author: .user.login, path, line, start_line, body}] | sort_by(.created_at)'
87	```
88	
89	For concise terminal output:
90	
91	```bash
92	gh api "/repos/$REPO/pulls/$PR/comments?per_page=100" \
93	  --jq '.[] | select(.created_at >= "'"$SINCE"'") | "PATH: \(.path):\(.line // .start_line // 0)\n\(.body)\n---"'
94	```
95	
96	## Fetch full details for compressed or truncated comments
97	
98	If a comment body appears compressed or incomplete, fetch the individual comment by ID:
99	
100	```bash
101	COMMENT_ID=1234567890
102	
103	gh api "/repos/$REPO/pulls/comments/$COMMENT_ID" \
104	  --jq '{body, diff_hunk, path, line, start_line}'
105	```
106	
107	This is more reliable than relying on truncated aggregate output.
108	
109	## Request Copilot review
110	
111	```bash
112	gh copilot-review "$PR" --repo "$REPO"
113	```
114	
115	If the extension is missing:
116	
117	```bash
118	gh extension install ChrisCarini/gh-copilot-review
119	```
120	
121	## Wait and poll after requesting review
122	
123	Manual sequence:
124	
125	```bash
126	sleep 240
127	
128	gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --json reviews,commits \
129	  --jq '{latestCommit: .commits[-1].committedDate, latestCopilot: ([.reviews[] | select(.author.login == "copilot-pull-request-reviewer") | {submittedAt,state,body}] | sort_by(.submittedAt) | reverse | .[0])}'
130	```
131	
132	If the latest Copilot review is still older than the latest commit, wait two minutes and check again. Repeat at most 10 times.
133	
134	## CodeRabbit review details
135	
136	CodeRabbit often stores details in the review body. Fetch the latest review body:
137	
138	```bash
139	gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --json reviews \
140	  --jq '[.reviews[] | select(.author.login == "coderabbitai") | {submittedAt,body}] | sort_by(.submittedAt) | reverse | .[0].body'
141	```
142	
143	Look for sections such as:
144	
145	- `Actionable comments posted`
146	- `Duplicate comments`
147	- `Nitpick comments`
148	
149	Prioritize actionable comments. Treat duplicates and nits as lower priority unless they point to a real bug.
150	
151	## Fix strategy
152	
153	Before editing, classify the comments:
154	
155	| Type | Action |
156	| --- | --- |
157	| Correctness/security/accessibility | Fix unless clearly false. |
158	| Repeated same pattern | Prefer one shared abstraction or guard. |
159	| Conflicting bot guidance | Stop and pick the best architecture. Document why. |
160	| Nit or copy polish | Fix only if low-risk and consistent with product language. |
161	| False positive | Leave code unchanged and consider replying on the PR. |
162	
163	When a reviewer keeps finding adjacent instances of the same issue, stop patching page by page. Search the codebase, design a single owner for the behavior, and remove duplicated logic.
164	
165	## Verification before commit
166	
167	Use repo-supported checks only:
168	
169	```bash
170	npm run format:lint
171	npm run build
172	npm run format:knip
173	npx prettier --check <changed-files>
174	npx cspell lint --quiet <changed-files>
175	git diff --check
176	```
177	
178	`npm run format` is the full check, but it can fail on unrelated untracked files. If that happens, verify the changed files directly and do not modify user-owned untracked files unless explicitly asked.
179	
180	## Commit and push safety
181	
182	Before every commit:
183	
184	```bash
185	git diff --cached
186	git status
187	git log --oneline -10
188	```
189	
190	Check staged changes for secrets, credentials, generated build outputs, and unrelated files.
191	
192	If a pre-commit hook fails because of an unrelated untracked file, do not stage or edit that file unless the user asked for it. It is acceptable to commit with `HUSKY=0` only after the staged changes have passed the relevant checks directly.
193	
194	```bash
195	git commit -m "fix(scope): concise message"
196	git push origin <branch>
197	```
198	
199	## Commenting or updating the PR
200	
201	```bash
202	# Add a PR comment from a prepared markdown file.
203	gh pr comment "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --body-file docs-dev/pr-body-text/<file>.md
204	
205	# Update PR description.
206	gh pr edit "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --body-file <file>
207	```
208	
209	## Tips
210	
211	- Run `gh auth status` if GitHub commands fail unexpectedly.
212	- Use the fork repo with `--repo` when the current branch belongs to a fork PR.
213	- Prefer `gh pr view --json ... --jq ...` for review metadata.
214	- Prefer `gh api /repos/$REPO/pulls/$PR/comments?per_page=100` for inline comments.
215	- Fetch individual comment IDs when aggregate output is compressed or truncated.
216	- Record the final clean state when Copilot reports no new comments.

## Goals

- Identify only the comments that belong to the latest review cycle.
- Verify each comment before changing code.
- Fix correctness, security, accessibility, and maintainability issues first.
- Avoid circular review loops by consolidating repeated patterns into one clean design.
- Stop when Copilot returns no new comments, or after 10 review-fix loops.

## Review loop policy

After requesting a Copilot review:

1. Wait 4 minutes, then check whether a newer Copilot review exists.
2. If it is not ready, wait up to 10 more times for 2 minutes each.
3. Once comments arrive, read the review summary and all new inline comments.
4. Validate each comment:
   - If it is correct, fix it.
   - If it is a nit only, consider whether it is worth changing.
   - If it conflicts with an earlier comment, stop and choose the cleaner architecture instead of toggling code back and forth.
   - If several comments share the same root cause, make one consolidated design fix.
5. Run the project verification commands appropriate for the changed files.
6. Commit, push, and request a new Copilot review.
7. Repeat up to 10 times.
8. Exit early when Copilot returns `generated no new comments`.

Do not continue an unbounded loop. If the 10-loop limit is reached and Copilot still reports issues, summarize the remaining pattern and recommend a deliberate consolidation pass.

## Review data model

- **Review event**: top-level review submission with timestamp and summary body.
- **Inline comment**: file-specific comment under `/pulls/<PR>/comments`.
- **Issue comment**: timeline comment under `/issues/<PR>/comments`.
- **Review body**: some bots, especially CodeRabbit, place nested actionable details in the review body instead of inline comments.

Inline comments can be associated with a later review event even if timestamps are close together. Always compare both commit time and review submission time.

## Quick setup

```bash
PR=2
REPO=$(gh repo view --json owner,name -q '.owner.login + "/" + .name')
```

For fork PRs, pass the repo explicitly when needed:

```bash
REPO=SvenMeyer/front-pro
PR=2
```

## Find the latest commit and reviews

```bash
# Latest local commit with timestamp.
git log --oneline -1 --pretty=format:'%h %ai %s'

# Latest PR commits from GitHub.
gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --json commits \
  --jq '.commits[-5:][] | {oid, committedDate, messageHeadline}'

# Latest Copilot reviews.
gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --json reviews \
  --jq '[.reviews[] | select(.author.login == "copilot-pull-request-reviewer") | {submittedAt,state,body}] | sort_by(.submittedAt) | reverse | .[0:5]'
```

A clean Copilot result looks like:

```text
Copilot reviewed X out of Y changed files in this pull request and generated no new comments.
```

## Fetch new Copilot comments

Use the review timestamp or latest pushed commit timestamp as the lower bound.

```bash
SINCE="2026-06-07T13:42:00Z"

gh api "/repos/$REPO/pulls/$PR/comments?per_page=100" \
  --jq '[.[] | select(.created_at >= "'"$SINCE"'" and (.user.login == "Copilot" or .user.login == "copilot-pull-request-reviewer")) | {id, created_at, updated_at, author: .user.login, path, line, start_line, body}] | sort_by(.created_at)'
```

For concise terminal output:

```bash
gh api "/repos/$REPO/pulls/$PR/comments?per_page=100" \
  --jq '.[] | select(.created_at >= "'"$SINCE"'") | "PATH: \(.path):\(.line // .start_line // 0)\n\(.body)\n---"'
```

## Fetch full details for compressed or truncated comments

If a comment body appears compressed or incomplete, fetch the individual comment by ID:

```bash
COMMENT_ID=1234567890

gh api "/repos/$REPO/pulls/comments/$COMMENT_ID" \
  --jq '{body, diff_hunk, path, line, start_line}'
```

This is more reliable than relying on truncated aggregate output.

## Request Copilot review

```bash
gh copilot-review "$PR" --repo "$REPO"
```

If the extension is missing:

```bash
gh extension install ChrisCarini/gh-copilot-review
```

## Wait and poll after requesting review

Manual sequence:

```bash
sleep 240

gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --json reviews,commits \
  --jq '{latestCommit: .commits[-1].committedDate, latestCopilot: ([.reviews[] | select(.author.login == "copilot-pull-request-reviewer") | {submittedAt,state,body}] | sort_by(.submittedAt) | reverse | .[0])}'
```

If the latest Copilot review is still older than the latest commit, wait two minutes and check again. Repeat at most 10 times.

## CodeRabbit review details

CodeRabbit often stores details in the review body. Fetch the latest review body:

```bash
gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --json reviews \
  --jq '[.reviews[] | select(.author.login == "coderabbitai") | {submittedAt,body}] | sort_by(.submittedAt) | reverse | .[0].body'
```

Look for sections such as:

- `Actionable comments posted`
- `Duplicate comments`
- `Nitpick comments`

Prioritize actionable comments. Treat duplicates and nits as lower priority unless they point to a real bug.

## Fix strategy

Before editing, classify the comments:

| Type | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Correctness/security/accessibility | Fix unless clearly false. |
| Repeated same pattern | Prefer one shared abstraction or guard. |
| Conflicting bot guidance | Stop and pick the best architecture. Document why. |
| Nit or copy polish | Fix only if low-risk and consistent with product language. |
| False positive | Leave code unchanged and consider replying on the PR. |

When a reviewer keeps finding adjacent instances of the same issue, stop patching page by page. Search the codebase, design a single owner for the behavior, and remove duplicated logic.

## Verification before commit

Use repo-supported checks only:

```bash
npm run format:lint
npm run build
npm run format:knip
npx prettier --check <changed-files>
npx cspell lint --quiet <changed-files>
git diff --check
```

`npm run format` is the full check, but it can fail on unrelated untracked files. If that happens, verify the changed files directly and do not modify user-owned untracked files unless explicitly asked.

## Commit and push safety

Before every commit:

```bash
git diff --cached
git status
git log --oneline -10
```

Check staged changes for secrets, credentials, generated build outputs, and unrelated files.

If a pre-commit hook fails because of an unrelated untracked file, do not stage or edit that file unless the user asked for it. It is acceptable to commit with `HUSKY=0` only after the staged changes have passed the relevant checks directly.

```bash
git commit -m "fix(scope): concise message"
git push origin <branch>
```

## Commenting or updating the PR

```bash
# Add a PR comment from a prepared markdown file.
gh pr comment "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --body-file docs-dev/pr-body-text/<file>.md

# Update PR description.
gh pr edit "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --body-file <file>
```

## Tips

- Run `gh auth status` if GitHub commands fail unexpectedly.
- Use the fork repo with `--repo` when the current branch belongs to a fork PR.
- Prefer `gh pr view --json ... --jq ...` for review metadata.
- Prefer `gh api /repos/$REPO/pulls/$PR/comments?per_page=100` for inline comments.
- Fetch individual comment IDs when aggregate output is compressed or truncated.
- Record the final clean state when Copilot reports no new comments.

content.text:
`high effort → 3+5 angles × 6 candidates → 1-vote verify (recall-biased) → ≤10 findings`

You are reviewing for **recall** at high effort: catch every real bug a careful
reviewer would catch in one sitting. At this level, catching real bugs matters
more than avoiding false positives. Err on the side of surfacing.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Find candidates (3 correctness angles + 3 cleanup angles + 1 altitude angle + 1 conventions angle, up to 6 each)

Run **8 independent finder angles** via the Agent tool. Each
surfaces **up to 6 candidate findings** with `file`, `line`, a one-line
`summary`, and a concrete `failure_scenario`.

### Angle A — line-by-line diff scan

Read every hunk in the diff, line by line. Then Read the enclosing function for
each hunk — bugs in unchanged lines of a touched function are in scope (the PR
re-exposes or fails to fix them). For every line ask: what input, state, timing,
or platform makes this line wrong? Look for inverted/wrong conditions,
off-by-one, null/undefined deref, missing `await`, falsy-zero checks,
wrong-variable copy-paste, error swallowed in catch, unescaped regex metachars.

### Angle B — removed-behavior auditor

For every line the diff DELETES or replaces, name the invariant or behavior it
enforced, then search the new code for where that invariant is re-established.
If you can't find it, that's a candidate: a removed guard, a dropped error
path, a narrowed validation, a deleted test that was covering a real case.

### Angle C — cross-file tracer

For each function the diff changes, find its callers (Grep for the symbol) and
check whether the change breaks any call site: a new precondition, a changed
return shape, a new exception, a timing/ordering dependency. Also check callees:
does a parallel change in the same PR make a call unsafe?

### Reuse

The angles above hunt for bugs; this one and the next two hunt for cleanup in
the changed code. Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

### Conventions (CLAUDE.md)

Find the CLAUDE.md files that govern the changed code: the user-level
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, the repo-root CLAUDE.md, plus any CLAUDE.md or
CLAUDE.local.md in a directory that is an ancestor of a changed file (a
directory's CLAUDE.md only applies to files at or below it). Read each one
that exists, then check the diff for clear violations of the rules they state.

Only flag a violation when you can quote the exact rule and the exact line
that breaks it — no style preferences, no vague "spirit of the doc"
inferences. In the finding, name the CLAUDE.md path and quote the rule so the
report can cite it. If no CLAUDE.md applies, return nothing for this angle.

Cleanup, altitude, and conventions candidates use the same
`file`/`line`/`summary` shape; in `failure_scenario`, state the concrete
cost (what is duplicated, wasted, harder to maintain, or which CLAUDE.md rule
is broken) instead of a crash. Correctness bugs always outrank cleanup,
altitude, and conventions findings when the output cap forces a cut.

Pass every candidate with a nameable failure scenario through — finders that
silently drop half-believed candidates bypass the verify step and are the
dominant cause of misses.

## Phase 2 — Verify (1-vote, recall-biased)

Dedup near-duplicates (same defect, same location, same reason → keep one). For
each remaining candidate, run **one verifier** via the Agent tool:
give it the diff, the relevant file(s), and the candidate; it returns exactly
one of **CONFIRMED / PLAUSIBLE / REFUTED**.

**PLAUSIBLE by default** — do not refute a candidate for being "speculative" or
"depends on runtime state" when the state is realistic: concurrency races,
nil/undefined on a rare-but-reachable path (error handler, cold cache, missing
optional field), falsy-zero treated as missing, off-by-one on a boundary the
code does not exclude, retry storms / partial failures, regex/allowlist that
lost an anchor. These are PLAUSIBLE.

**REFUTED** only when constructible from the code: factually wrong (quote the
actual line); provably impossible (type/constant/invariant — show it); already
handled in this diff (cite the guard); or pure style with no observable effect.

Keep **CONFIRMED and PLAUSIBLE**. Drop REFUTED.

## Output

Return findings as a JSON array of at most 10 objects:

```json
[
  {
    "file": "path/to/file.ext",
    "line": 123,
    "summary": "one-sentence statement of the bug",
    "failure_scenario": "concrete inputs/state → wrong output/crash"
  }
]
```

Ranked most-severe first. If more than 10 survive, keep the 10 most
severe. If nothing survives verification, return `[]`.

cat > /tmp/pr-body.md <<'EOF'
## What & why

Implements **BRD Epic 4 — Primary Subscription & Settlement (atomic DvP)** for issue #3. A Subscriber buys Fraction Tokens in a primary offering paying a **mock regulated stablecoin**, settled as **atomic delivery-versus-payment**: stablecoin → Vendor and freshly minted ERC-3643 Fraction Tokens → Subscriber in one transaction, or the whole thing reverts.

Built Ctrl Alt-independent behind mock-as-interface seams (ADR-0004, ADR-0005). The stablecoin + fiat ramp is the only mock and is tracked for replacement by **#12**.

## Contracts (`packages/contracts`)

- **`MockStablecoin`** — ERC-20 cash leg (6dp) with an open faucet simulating the fiat on-ramp (Ctrl Alt seam #12). The DvP contract depends only on `IERC20`, never on the mock.
- **`PrimaryOffering`** — atomic DvP. Per-cell offering params (unit price, discount, optional platform fee, total cap, per-investor limit). `subscribe()` pulls stablecoin to the Vendor (+ fee to the fee recipient) and mints Fraction Tokens to the caller; the ERC-3643 compliance check on the delivery leg reverts (unwinding the cash leg) when the buyer isn't whitelisted/verified or is frozen. CEI + `ReentrancyGuard`. Emits `Subscribed` + `ProceedsReleased` for reconciliation (FR4.3).
- **`DeployOffering.s.sol`** — deploys the rail, grants the offering the token agent role so it can mint, and creates a demo offering.

## Web (`apps/web`)

- Settlement **read-model** in Neon (+ in-memory fallback) behind one interface, mirroring the existing records pattern; pure **cost-basis aggregation** (`aggregateHoldings`, test-first).
- **`/api/portfolio`** — record a confirmed settlement; return holdings + history.
- **`SubscriptionPanel`** — live price/discount/fees/balance, approve + DvP confirm (FR4.5); snapshots the submitted order so the persisted settlement matches the on-chain tx.
- **`Portfolio`** — holdings, cost basis, settlement history (FR4.6).

## Acceptance criteria (issue #3)

- [x] Mock stablecoin + DvP subscription contract; buy is atomic (token+cash or revert), tested
- [x] Per-cell offering parameters (price/discount, caps, limits) enforced
- [x] Vendor receives proceeds on settlement
- [x] Subscription UI shows price/discount/fees/balance and confirms DvP
- [x] Portfolio reflects holdings + cost basis; settlement events emitted

## Deferred (out of scope, noted in code)

- Escrowed/conditional settlement + fiat-wire fallback leg (FR4.2/FR4.8) → governance windows, Epic 7.
- Real Ctrl Alt stablecoin + fiat on/off-ramp + reconciliation webhooks → **#12**.

## Tests

- **Foundry: 28 pass** (14 new in `PrimaryOffering.t.sol`, against a real ERC-3643 suite): atomic happy path, revert unwinds cash on failed delivery (non-whitelisted / insufficient balance), cap & per-investor enforcement, discount/fee math, access control, fuzz.
- **Web: 15 pass** (cost-basis aggregation + settlements repo). Typecheck + lint clean. `forge fmt --check` clean.

Closes #3.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

## Implementation complete — issue #3 (Epic 4: Primary Subscription & atomic DvP)

**Contracts** (`packages/contracts`)
- `MockStablecoin` — ERC-20 cash leg + faucet (Ctrl Alt seam #12)
- `PrimaryOffering` — atomic DvP: stablecoin→Vendor (+ optional fee) and mint Fraction Tokens→Subscriber in one tx or revert; per-cell price/discount/fee/cap/per-investor limit; `Subscribed`+`ProceedsReleased` events; CEI + ReentrancyGuard
- `DeployOffering.s.sol` — deploys rail, grants token-agent role, creates demo offering

- Settlement read-model (Neon + in-memory behind one interface), pure cost-basis aggregation (test-first), `/api/portfolio`, `SubscriptionPanel`, `Portfolio` — **15 web tests** pass; typecheck/lint/`forge fmt` clean

## Decisions I made on my own (as you asked)

1. **Interpreted #3 as Epic 4 (DvP subscription)**, not its stale title ("Cell creation + Diamond Token issuance" = Epic 3). The body, acceptance criteria, and "Refs: BRD v2 Epic 4" all describe DvP; I built to those.
2. **Delivery = primary mint** (offering holds token-agent role), not transfer of pre-minted inventory — the accurate model for a *primary* offering, and it avoids giving the offering its own whitelisted ONCHAINID.
3. **Proceeds go straight to the Vendor on settlement** (no escrow). Escrow/conditional + fiat-wire fallback (FR4.2/FR4.8) are governance-window concerns I deferred to Epic 7, noted in code.
4. **New branch + PR** rather than reusing the issue-#2 branch (you'd flagged the branch might be missing).
5. **Left `AGENTS-PR-review.md` untracked/uncommitted** — it's user-owned guidance, per its own rules.
6. Added a faucet button + 6dp `mUSD` to make the flow demoable without Ctrl Alt rails.

I'll continue the review-fix loop automatically once Copilot (and any other bots) report back.

=== INLINE comments (all bots) ===
### kilo-code-bot[bot] — apps/web/lib/db/schema.sql:28 [id 3447657301]
**SUGGESTION:** `subscription_settlements` has no uniqueness guard on `tx_hash`, and `NeonSettlementsRepository.add` / `InMemorySettlementsRepository.add` blindly insert every row. Because `aggregateHoldings` sums `quantity` and `totalPaid` per token, a duplicate row for the same confirmed DvP (e.g. a retried/re-sent persistence request from the `SubscriptionPanel` effect, or any re-POST) double-counts the subscriber's holdings and cost basis. Unlike `registry_records` (a flat append-only log), this table feeds a financial aggregation, so consider a `UNIQUE` constraint on `(chain_id, tx_hash)` plus idempotent handling in `add()` (return the existing row on conflict) so the projection can't be duplicated.

---
Reply with `@kilocode-bot fix it` to have Kilo Code address this issue.

### chatgpt-codex-connector[bot] — .github/workflows/ci.yml:30 [id 3447657870]
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Install npm dependencies before Foundry builds**

In the contracts workflow, a clean runner reaches this step after only checkout and `Install Foundry`; no `pnpm install` has run in this job. The Solidity imports are remapped to `node_modules/...` in `packages/contracts/foundry.toml`, and those packages are npm dependencies in `packages/contracts/package.json` rather than submodules, so `forge build --sizes` cannot resolve `@openzeppelin`, `@tokenysolutions`, or `@onchain-id` on every PR. Add a pnpm setup/install step before running Forge.

### chatgpt-codex-connector[bot] — apps/web/app/api/portfolio/route.ts:77 [id 3447657873]
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Verify settlement transactions before saving rows**

On the public POST path, the route only validates the payload shape before persisting the caller-supplied investor, token, amounts, and `txHash`. Because `GET /api/portfolio` derives holdings and cost basis directly from these rows, anyone who can call `/api/portfolio` can forge or duplicate a settlement for any wallet without a confirmed on-chain `Subscribed` event. Verify the receipt/log against `PrimaryOffering` before `repo.add(record)`.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

### Copilot — apps/web/lib/portfolio/holdings.ts:46 [id 3447658287]
`Array.sort` comparator never returns `0` when `totalCost` values are equal, which can lead to inconsistent ordering (and potentially flaky UI/tests). Handle the equality case explicitly.

### Copilot — packages/contracts/script/DeployOffering.s.sol:65 [id 3447658300]
`discountBps`/`feeBps` are read as `uint256` and then down-cast to `uint16` without validating the raw env value first. If someone sets (e.g.) `OFFERING_DISCOUNT_BPS=70000`, the `uint16` cast will wrap to `4464` and silently deploy an unintended configuration.

### Copilot — apps/web/app/api/portfolio/route.ts:46 [id 3447658306]
`txHash` is only checked for non-empty string. Since this route writes to the persistence layer, it should at least validate a proper 32-byte transaction hash format (0x + 64 hex chars) to prevent storing arbitrary garbage.

### Copilot — apps/web/app/api/records/route.ts:23 [id 3447658309]
`updatedBy` and `txHash` are accepted as arbitrary strings. Since this endpoint writes to the backing store, validate `updatedBy` as an address and `txHash` as a 32-byte hex hash to avoid polluting the DB with invalid values.

### Copilot — apps/web/app/api/portfolio/route.ts:78 [id 3447658310]
This endpoint accepts client-supplied settlement details and persists them without verifying that `txHash` is a real on-chain `Subscribed` event (or that it matches the payload). As a result, anyone can POST arbitrary settlements into the read-model. Consider validating the tx receipt/logs (or gating writes behind auth) before inserting.

### Copilot — apps/web/components/SubscriptionPanel.tsx:149 [id 3447658319]
The portfolio persistence POST is not checked for success; if `/api/portfolio` fails (DB down/validation error), the UI still dispatches the settlement event and later renders a success message implying the portfolio updated. Check `res.ok` and only refresh/dispatch on success (or surface an error).

content.thinking:
Looking at the schema, there's a critical issue with the transaction hash not having a uniqueness constraint—duplicate POST requests could double-count holdings and cost basis. I need to add a UNIQUE constraint on the (chain_id, tx_hash) pair and make the add() operation idempotent using ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, plus deduplicate in the in-memory repository as well.

The CI configuration is missing an npm install step before the Foundry build, since the remappings reference node_modules—this would cause the build to fail. I should add pnpm install before running forge build in the contracts job.

The settlement transaction verification is the biggest concern: the POST endpoint is unauthenticated and unverified, so anyone could forge settlements. The right fix is to verify the txHash on-chain server-side by fetching the receipt, confirming it succeeded, and validating that it contains a Subscribed log from the configured PrimaryOffering address matching the payload details. This makes the read-model trustworthy, removes the forgery vector, and also addresses the tx_hash format validation and duplicate issues. I'll implement server-side verification in the port.

For the verification logic, I need to fetch the transaction receipt, decode the Subscribed event logs from the offering contract address, and compare the decoded data against the payload. The offering contract addresses are available server-side through the same environment variables used on the client. I'll create a dedicated verifier module that handles this check and gates persistence on successful verification—if the offering config isn't available for the chain, the verification fails and the request is rejected.

The key insight is to derive the persisted record directly from the on-chain event data rather than trusting the client-supplied amounts. The Subscribed event contains offeringId, investor, quantity, netToVendor, fee, and totalPaid. I can verify the investor matches the connected wallet, and I'll need to fetch the token address from the offering contract itself via getOffering(offeringId) to get the authoritative token. The vendor can be cross-checked against ProceedsReleased events if needed, but the core strategy is to reconstruct the canonical record from the chain and persist that.

I'm also noting several other issues to fix: the sort comparator in holdings.ts that never returns 0, validation of basis points in the deployment script before casting to uint16, adding a txHash format check in the portfolio route, and validating the updatedBy and txHash fields in the records route.

For the UI, I need to check the response status in SubscriptionPanel.tsx before showing success—currently it displays success even if the persistence fails. And there's still the idempotency problem with settlements: even with on-chain verification, posting the same transaction twice would create duplicate rows, so I need to add a UNIQUE constraint on (chain_id, tx_hash) with an ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING clause to prevent double-counting.

Now let me examine the CI configuration and records route to understand what validation needs to be added there.

content.thinking:
The contracts job is missing the pnpm setup and node installation steps before running forge build, which causes it to fail resolving OpenZeppelin dependencies since the remappings point to node_modules that don't exist. I need to add pnpm install at the repository root before the forge build step so that the workspace dependencies get properly installed into packages/contracts/node_modules.

I'll add the pnpm action setup, Node.js setup with pnpm caching, and a frozen lockfile install at the repo root before the Build step. Since the job's default working directory is packages/contracts, I'll explicitly override the working directory for the install step to run from the repository root. pnpm will detect the workspace and install everything correctly, populating the node_modules where forge needs it.

Now I'm looking at the records/route.ts file to validate the updatedBy and txHash fields — I need to add address validation for updatedBy and check the transaction hash format.

I'm designing a settlement verification module that will create a public client, fetch the transaction receipt to confirm it succeeded, and parse the event logs from the offering contract to verify the settlement details match what was submitted.

Building verification logic... Building the settlement record...

The route will accept the full payload for backward compatibility with the component, but only extract the four required fields—chainId, offeringId, investor, and txHash—then re-derive everything else from the chain. I'll simplify the parseBody validation to just those four fields and make the amounts and token optional/ignored.

For idempotency in Neon, I'm adding a UNIQUE constraint on (chain_id, tx_hash) and using an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT approach to handle duplicate submissions gracefully.

- **Smaller, clearly-correct**: holdings sort comparator, deploy-script bps validation, records-route validation, and the UI `res.ok` check.

-- Off-chain Register read-model (ADR-0006: Neon / Postgres).
-- The NeonRecordsRepository creates this lazily; this file documents the schema
-- and can be applied manually (psql "$DATABASE_URL" -f lib/db/schema.sql).
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS registry_records (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  chain_id    BIGINT      NOT NULL,
  note        TEXT        NOT NULL,
  tx_hash     TEXT        NOT NULL,
  updated_by  TEXT        NOT NULL,
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Primary-subscription settlement read-model (issue #3, BRD FR4.3/FR4.6).
-- One row per confirmed DvP subscription; the portfolio (holdings + cost basis + history) is
-- derived from these rows. Amounts are NUMERIC(78,0) so 256-bit on-chain values round-trip.
-- NeonSettlementsRepository creates this lazily.
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS subscription_settlements (
  id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  chain_id      BIGINT        NOT NULL,
  offering_id   BIGINT        NOT NULL,
  token         TEXT          NOT NULL,
  investor      TEXT          NOT NULL,
  vendor        TEXT          NOT NULL,
  quantity      NUMERIC(78,0) NOT NULL,
  net_to_vendor NUMERIC(78,0) NOT NULL,
  fee           NUMERIC(78,0) NOT NULL,
  total_paid    NUMERIC(78,0) NOT NULL,
  tx_hash       TEXT          NOT NULL,
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ   NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

fix: address PR review (security, idempotency, CI, validation)

Resolves the Copilot, CodeRabbit/kilo-code and Codex review comments on #14:

- Portfolio POST no longer trusts client input: verifySettlement re-derives the
  settlement from the on-chain `Subscribed` event (receipt status, log from the
  configured PrimaryOffering, matching offering/investor) and reads token/vendor
  from the contract. Forged or mismatched settlements are rejected (422). Fixes
  the "anyone can POST arbitrary settlements" finding (Codex P1 + Copilot).
- Settlement persistence is idempotent on (chain_id, tx_hash): unique index +
  ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (Neon) and a dedupe guard (in-memory), so a retried
  POST can't double-count holdings/cost basis (kilo-code). Tests added.
- CI: install the pnpm workspace before `forge build`/`test`; the ERC-3643 libs
  resolve through node_modules remappings, not submodules (Codex P1).
- DeployOffering: validate discount/fee bps <= 10000 before the uint16 cast so
  an out-of-range env can't silently wrap (Copilot).
- aggregateHoldings: stable tie-break when totalCost is equal (Copilot).
- records + portfolio routes: validate txHash format and addresses (Copilot).
- SubscriptionPanel: check res.ok and surface a recording error instead of
  always showing success (Copilot).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git push 2>&1 | tail -3

## Wait and poll after requesting review

Manual sequence:

```bash
sleep 240

gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --json reviews,commits \
  --jq '{latestCommit: .commits[-1].committedDate, latestCopilot: ([.reviews[] | select(.author.login == "copilot-pull-request-reviewer") | {submittedAt,state,body}] | sort_by(.submittedAt) | reverse | .[0])}'
```

If the latest Copilot review is still older than the latest commit, wait two minutes and check again. Repeat at most 10 times.

### Automated poll loop (zsh-safe)

When scripting the wait, **do not compare ISO-8601 timestamps with the shell `test`/`[ ]`
operators.** `[ "$LATEST" \> "$SINCE" ]` fails under zsh with `condition expected: >` (zsh does
not accept `\>` as a `test` string-comparison operator, and an unescaped `>` would redirect to a
file). Let **jq** do the timestamp comparison (its `>` is a proper lexicographic string compare on
the sortable ISO-8601 values) and let the shell do only a **numeric** `-gt` test.

Also note `gh pr view --jq` does **not** support jq `--arg`; pipe `gh ... --json` output to a
standalone `jq --arg` instead.

```bash
PR=14
REPO=SvenMeyer/roughnet-v1
SINCE="$(gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --json commits --jq '.commits[-1].committedDate')"

# Poll for a Copilot review newer than the latest commit (4 min, then up to 10×2 min).
sleep 240
for i in $(seq 1 10); do
  NEW=$(gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --json reviews \
    | jq --arg since "$SINCE" \
        '[.reviews[] | select(.author.login=="copilot-pull-request-reviewer" and .submittedAt > $since)] | length')
  if [ "$NEW" -gt 0 ]; then
    echo "New Copilot review present (count=$NEW)"
    break
  fi
  sleep 120
done
```

The same jq-compares / shell-numeric-tests rule applies to any bot (`coderabbitai`,
`chatgpt-codex-connector`, `kilo-code-bot`, …) — swap the `.author.login` filter.

# PR Review Handling Guide

Use this guide when working through automated PR feedback from Copilot, CodeRabbit, Vercel, Qodo, or similar reviewers.

## Goals

- Identify only the comments that belong to the latest review cycle.
- Verify each comment before changing code.
- Fix correctness, security, accessibility, and maintainability issues first.
- Avoid circular review loops by consolidating repeated patterns into one clean design.
- Stop when Copilot returns no new comments, or after 10 review-fix loops.

## Review loop policy

After requesting a Copilot review:

1. Wait 4 minutes, then check whether a newer Copilot review exists.
2. If it is not ready, wait up to 10 more times for 2 minutes each.
3. Once comments arrive, read the review summary and all new inline comments.
4. Validate each comment:
   - If it is correct, fix it.
   - If it is a nit only, consider whether it is worth changing.
   - If it conflicts with an earlier comment, stop and choose the cleaner architecture instead of toggling code back and forth.
   - If several comments share the same root cause, make one consolidated design fix.
5. Run the project verification commands appropriate for the changed files.
6. Commit, push, and request a new Copilot review.
7. Repeat up to 10 times.
8. Exit early when Copilot returns `generated no new comments`.

Do not continue an unbounded loop. If the 10-loop limit is reached and Copilot still reports issues, summarize the remaining pattern and recommend a deliberate consolidation pass.

## Review data model

- **Review event**: top-level review submission with timestamp and summary body.
- **Inline comment**: file-specific comment under `/pulls/<PR>/comments`.
- **Issue comment**: timeline comment under `/issues/<PR>/comments`.
- **Review body**: some bots, especially CodeRabbit, place nested actionable details in the review body instead of inline comments.

Inline comments can be associated with a later review event even if timestamps are close together. Always compare both commit time and review submission time.

## Quick setup

```bash
PR=2
REPO=$(gh repo view --json owner,name -q '.owner.login + "/" + .name')
```

For fork PRs, pass the repo explicitly when needed:

```bash
REPO=SvenMeyer/front-pro
PR=2
```

## Find the latest commit and reviews

```bash
# Latest local commit with timestamp.
git log --oneline -1 --pretty=format:'%h %ai %s'

# Latest PR commits from GitHub.
gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --json commits \
  --jq '.commits[-5:][] | {oid, committedDate, messageHeadline}'

# Latest Copilot reviews.
gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --json reviews \
  --jq '[.reviews[] | select(.author.login == "copilot-pull-request-reviewer") | {submittedAt,state,body}] | sort_by(.submittedAt) | reverse | .[0:5]'
```

A clean Copilot result looks like:

```text
Copilot reviewed X out of Y changed files in this pull request and generated no new comments.
```

## Fetch new Copilot comments

Use the review timestamp or latest pushed commit timestamp as the lower bound.

```bash
SINCE="2026-06-07T13:42:00Z"

gh api "/repos/$REPO/pulls/$PR/comments?per_page=100" \
  --jq '[.[] | select(.created_at >= "'"$SINCE"'" and (.user.login == "Copilot" or .user.login == "copilot-pull-request-reviewer")) | {id, created_at, updated_at, author: .user.login, path, line, start_line, body}] | sort_by(.created_at)'
```

For concise terminal output:

```bash
gh api "/repos/$REPO/pulls/$PR/comments?per_page=100" \
  --jq '.[] | select(.created_at >= "'"$SINCE"'") | "PATH: \(.path):\(.line // .start_line // 0)\n\(.body)\n---"'
```

## Fetch full details for compressed or truncated comments

If a comment body appears compressed or incomplete, fetch the individual comment by ID:

```bash
COMMENT_ID=1234567890

gh api "/repos/$REPO/pulls/comments/$COMMENT_ID" \
  --jq '{body, diff_hunk, path, line, start_line}'
```

This is more reliable than relying on truncated aggregate output.

## Request Copilot review

```bash
gh copilot-review "$PR" --repo "$REPO"
```

If the extension is missing:

```bash
gh extension install ChrisCarini/gh-copilot-review
```

## Wait and poll after requesting review

Manual sequence:

```bash
sleep 240

gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --json reviews,commits \
  --jq '{latestCommit: .commits[-1].committedDate, latestCopilot: ([.reviews[] | select(.author.login == "copilot-pull-request-reviewer") | {submittedAt,state,body}] | sort_by(.submittedAt) | reverse | .[0])}'
```

If the latest Copilot review is still older than the latest commit, wait two minutes and check again. Repeat at most 10 times.

## CodeRabbit review details

CodeRabbit often stores details in the review body. Fetch the latest review body:

```bash
gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --json reviews \
  --jq '[.reviews[] | select(.author.login == "coderabbitai") | {submittedAt,body}] | sort_by(.submittedAt) | reverse | .[0].body'
```

Look for sections such as:

- `Actionable comments posted`
- `Duplicate comments`
- `Nitpick comments`

Prioritize actionable comments. Treat duplicates and nits as lower priority unless they point to a real bug.

## Fix strategy

Before editing, classify the comments:

| Type | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Correctness/security/accessibility | Fix unless clearly false. |
| Repeated same pattern | Prefer one shared abstraction or guard. |
| Conflicting bot guidance | Stop and pick the best architecture. Document why. |
| Nit or copy polish | Fix only if low-risk and consistent with product language. |
| False positive | Leave code unchanged and consider replying on the PR. |

When a reviewer keeps finding adjacent instances of the same issue, stop patching page by page. Search the codebase, design a single owner for the behavior, and remove duplicated logic.

## Verification before commit

Use repo-supported checks only:

```bash
npm run format:lint
npm run build
npm run format:knip
npx prettier --check <changed-files>
npx cspell lint --quiet <changed-files>
git diff --check
```

`npm run format` is the full check, but it can fail on unrelated untracked files. If that happens, verify the changed files directly and do not modify user-owned untracked files unless explicitly asked.

## Commit and push safety

Before every commit:

```bash
git diff --cached
git status
git log --oneline -10
```

Check staged changes for secrets, credentials, generated build outputs, and unrelated files.

If a pre-commit hook fails because of an unrelated untracked file, do not stage or edit that file unless the user asked for it. It is acceptable to commit with `HUSKY=0` only after the staged changes have passed the relevant checks directly.

```bash
git commit -m "fix(scope): concise message"
git push origin <branch>
```

## Commenting or updating the PR

```bash
# Add a PR comment from a prepared markdown file.
gh pr comment "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --body-file docs-dev/pr-body-text/<file>.md

# Update PR description.
gh pr edit "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --body-file <file>
```

## Tips

- Run `gh auth status` if GitHub commands fail unexpectedly.
- Use the fork repo with `--repo` when the current branch belongs to a fork PR.
- Prefer `gh pr view --json ... --jq ...` for review metadata.
- Prefer `gh api /repos/$REPO/pulls/$PR/comments?per_page=100` for inline comments.
- Fetch individual comment IDs when aggregate output is compressed or truncated.
- Record the final clean state when Copilot reports no new comments.

`parseClaim` validates `offeringId` but does not validate `chainId` beyond `typeof === "number"`. A non-integer/negative/NaN chainId can slip through and then be persisted (or cause confusing 501s). Mirror the stricter validation used in `/api/records` by requiring an integer, positive `chainId`.

`verifyNoteUpdate` selects `events[0]` when multiple `NoteUpdated` logs exist in the same tx. Since the DB schema is idempotent on `(chainId, txHash)`, persisting an arbitrary event can record the wrong note if a transaction emits multiple updates. Consider rejecting transactions with 0 or >1 matching events to avoid ambiguous persistence.

`verifySettlement` uses `events.find(...)` and assumes at most one matching `Subscribed` event per transaction. file.content:
name: CI

on:
  push:
  pull_request:

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  contracts:
    name: Contracts (Foundry)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: packages/contracts
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          submodules: recursive

      - name: Install Foundry
        uses: foundry-rs/foundry-toolchain@v1

      # The ERC-3643/ONCHAINID/OpenZeppelin libraries are npm deps resolved through
      # foundry.toml remappings into node_modules (not git submodules), so forge build/test
      # need the workspace installed first.
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
        with:
          version: 10

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: pnpm

      - name: Install dependencies
        working-directory: ${{ github.workspace }}
        run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      - name: Check formatting
        run: forge fmt --check

      - name: Build
        run: forge build --sizes

      - name: Test
        run: forge test -vvv

  web:
    name: Web (Next.js)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
        with:
          version: 10

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: pnpm

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      - name: Typecheck
        run: pnpm --filter @roughnet/web typecheck

      - name: Lint
        run: pnpm --filter @roughnet/web lint

      - name: Test
        run: pnpm --filter @roughnet/web test

      - name: Build
        run: pnpm --filter @roughnet/web build
